newsitem.title: USA: Jury in Florida tobacco trial to resume deliberations.
newsitem.headline: Jury in Florida tobacco trial to resume deliberations.

text.p: In a critical week for the cigarette industry, a Florida jury resumes deliberations in a wrongful death lawsuit on Monday as unrelated settlement talks continue between tobacco firms and state officials.
Jurors were to begin discussions at 9 a.m. EDT Monday. They met for nearly two hours after closing arguments but were unable to reach a verdict before adjourning for the weekend.

The six-member panel, five women and one man, have been asked to decide whether R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., manufacturered a defective and dangerous product and negligently contributed to the death of Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who died at 49 of lung cancer.

Connor filed a product liability lawsuit against Reynolds about six months before she died in October 1995. Her sister, Dana Raulerson, then took up the suit as a wrongful death action on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children.
"I would not want to have to predict an outcome," Smith Barney tobacco analyst Martin Feldman, who watched the trial closely, said after the jury began deliberations.

While the trial has been widely followed -- industry stock analysts and tobacco litigators attended many court sessions during the four weeks it took to try the case -- there have been differing views on the potential impact of its outcome.

Some have argued that another victory for Raulerson's folksy Jacksonville lawyer, Norwood "Woody" Wilner -- who last August won a $750,000 judgment in a smoker's product liability case against B.A.T Industries Plc's Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp -- would herald a trend and prove that tobacco liability cases are winnable.

Others have said the trial, while important, pales in comparison to settlement talks set to resume as early as Monday between the industry state attorneys general over Medicaid lawsuits, and to the April 25 decision of a U.S. District Court judge in North Carolina that the Food and Drug Administration can regulate tobacco as a drug.
Feldman said while the settlement talks were much more important to the future of tobacco stocks, a loss for Reynolds at the trial would certainly cause concern among investors.
In the short term, "stocks might fall further on a (Reynolds) loss than they might go up on a win," Feldman said.

In the closing days of the Florida trial, even Wilner tried to downplay its importance, saying the idiosyncrasies of juries could take any case either way, but the industry had received clear messages in the Brown & Williamson case and the FDA ruling that it needed to come to grips with its liability.
"The industry has to deal with it. They've got to get serious about compensating their victims," he said.
Jacksonville, a verdant city on the St. Johns River in northeast Florida, might seem an unlikely apex for the battle against Big Tobacco.

But from a small office near the Duval County Courthouse, Wilner and his colleagues have launched a fearsome assault against the giants of the industry. The Brown & Williamson judgment was just the second monetary award ever against the industry, and Wilner estimated he has filed more than 300 such individual liability and wrongful death cases.
"We oppose any attempt to grant blanket immunity to the cigarette industry," he said.
Wilner told jurors they could send a message by punishing Reynolds for making it "cool to smoke poison."
In a methodical closing argument, Reynolds' lawyer Paul Crist reiterated tobacco's tried and true defense: that smokers choose to smoke, making the responsibility theirs.

While the industry has denied for decades that nicotine is addictive and that the alleged link between smoking and various ailments has been proved, Reynolds found itself in the unusual position in this trial of entering evidence to show that everyone has known the dangers of smoking for decades.
The company went so far as to play to jurors a 1947 Tex Williams song, "Smoke, Smoke, Smoke That Cigarette," that says: "puff, puff, puff until you smoke yourself to death."
"Each one of us has to make lifestyle choices," Crist said. "Mrs. Connor chose to smoke and she chose to continue."
The jurors showed little emotion during closing arguments, even during an impassioned plea from Wilner colleague Ron Motley to punish Reynolds for the loss suffered by Connor's three children.

But one former juror said she would not award damages against Reynolds. Sandra Grant, who was excused from the jury two-and-a-half weeks into the trial because of a family illness, told the Florida Times-Union that Connor knew what she was doing was dangerous and chose to do it anyway.
